title: Gerson: every offense against God is of itself deadly; veniality is mercy
source_text: XI. Etenim nonnulli sunt inter Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, & quidem non infimae notae, qui docent omnia peccata juste a Deo morte aeterna puniri posse; quod vero quaedam eorum ad poenam solummodo temporalem imputantur, nec mortis aeternae reatum in peccantem inducunt, & idcirco a peccatis mortalibus distinguuntur, id tribuendum esse Dei clementiae atque indulgentiae, quae hac in parte toto suo jure erga hominem uti non vult. Haec est sententia Joannis illius Gerson, qui ante annos plus minus ducentos sexaginta Academiae Parisiensis Cancellarius fuit, & inter Theologos Sorbonicos celeberrimus, quam prolixe tradit & tuetur in tractatu quem inscribit de Vita Spirituali, lectione prima. Ubi agens de quidditate & quantificatione peccatorum, ut loquitur, hanc ponit conclusionem, Omne peccatum, pro quanto est offensa Dei, & contra legem ejus aeternam, est de sua conditione & indignitate mortiferum, secundum rigorem justitiae, & a vita gloriae separativum.
pass_a_gloss: For there are some among the doctors of the Roman Church, and indeed of no mean note, who teach that all sins can justly be punished by God with eternal death; but that some of them are imputed only to temporal punishment and do not bring upon the sinner the guilt of eternal death, and are therefore distinguished from mortal sins, is to be attributed to God’s clemency and indulgence, which in this part does not wish to use His whole right toward the person. This is the opinion of that John Gerson, who about two hundred sixty years ago was Chancellor of the University of Paris and most celebrated among the Sorbonne theologians, which he treats and defends at length in the treatise he entitles On the Spiritual Life, lecture one. Where, treating of the quiddity and quantification of sins, as he speaks, he lays down this conclusion: Every sin, insofar as it is an offense of God and against His eternal law, is of its own condition and unworthiness deadly, according to the rigor of justice, and separative from the life of glory.
pass_b_english: Gerson and allies: every sin could justly earn eternal death; milder imputation is God’s clemency, not the act’s own mildness.
He concludes that any offense against God is of itself deadly and cuts off from glory under justice’s rigor.

choices.why: Gerson’s claim that every offense is of itself lethal.
